title: Why Your Car Uses More Fuel Than It Should
hook: Measure the change, check the simple causes, then diagnose the evidence.

sections.heading: Measure before replacing parts
sections.body: Use a full-tank calculation over two or three comparable refills. Dashboard estimates move with traffic, wind, slopes and recent idling.

sections.heading: Set cold tire pressure correctly
sections.body: Use the pressure on the driver-door label, not the maximum on the tire sidewall. Repeated pressure loss needs inspection.

sections.heading: Smooth driving saves repeated work
sections.body: Rapid acceleration demands high power. Late braking throws away speed that fuel already created. Look ahead and leave space.

sections.heading: High speed increases air resistance
sections.body: Fuel economy normally falls as highway speed rises. Use a safe steady speed and compare the same car on similar routes.

sections.heading: Idling gives zero distance
sections.body: Air conditioning may be necessary in extreme heat, but forgotten waiting time still burns fuel without moving the car.

sections.heading: Short trips keep systems inefficient
sections.body: A cold engine and transmission have more friction. Combining errands can reduce repeated warm-up periods.

sections.heading: Air conditioning is a real load
sections.body: Vent trapped heat briefly, then use recirculation once the cabin begins cooling. Comfort and visibility remain the priority.

sections.heading: Weight and roof cargo matter
sections.body: Permanent boot clutter costs energy during acceleration. Unused roof boxes and racks also disturb airflow at highway speed.

sections.heading: Read warning lights properly
sections.body: A fault code identifies a system or condition, not automatically a failed part. Diagnose the cause before buying components.

sections.heading: Use the specified oil and fuel
sections.body: More expensive is not automatically better. Follow the engine-oil specification and octane requirement in the owner manual.

sections.heading: Check for mechanical drag
sections.body: Pulling, a hot wheel, abnormal wear, vibration or poor coasting can point to brakes, alignment, bearings, tires or transmission problems.

sections.heading: Run a controlled seven-day test
sections.body: Correct pressure, remove unused cargo, drive smoothly and log two tanks. If the loss remains, take the evidence to a technician.

callToAction: Check all four tires cold and start a two-tank fuel log.

shorts.hook: Stop using the tire sidewall number
shorts.body: The sidewall shows a tire limit. Your normal cold pressure is listed on the driver-door label or in the owner manual.
shorts.cta: Check all four tires before driving.

shorts.hook: Your fuel-economy display can mislead you
shorts.body: Traffic, hills, wind and recent idling can change the dashboard estimate fast. Confirm the trend with full-tank calculations.
shorts.cta: Compare at least two similar tanks.

shorts.hook: Hard braking wastes fuel you already burned
shorts.body: Late braking throws away speed. Leave space, look farther ahead and release the accelerator earlier when traffic slows.

shorts.hook: A fault code is not a parts order
shorts.body: The code points to a detected condition or system. Test the cause before replacing a sensor, valve or other component.
Set cold tire pressure, remove unused cargo, drive normally but smoothly, avoid forgotten idling and calculate the next refill.
shorts.cta: Repeat once before judging the result.
